newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks end slightly up, blue chips rebound.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks end slightly up, blue chips rebound.

text.p: A late buying of primary blue chips by onshore funds helped the Seoul stock market close slightly higher on Tuesday but brokers said the market needed further consolidation.
Banking shares were hit hard by the government's announcement to keep the current four percent ceiling of individual shareholding in commerical banks.
Kia Group shares were mixed on the news that its chairman asked finance minister Kang Kyong-shik to maintain its credit lines open and the group would seek to restructure.
The composite stock index rose 0.65 of a point to 753.70.

Choi Dong-chul at Ssangyong Securities said onshore funds boosted core blue chips, which no shares remained available to foreigners. SK Telecom rose 7,000 won to 441,000 and Samsung Electronics gained 900 won to 69,400.
Casey Choe at Union Bank of Switzerland said the yen's strength, an economic turnaround and interest rates had not been as favourable for the market as investors had earlier expected.

South Korean businesses expect a sluggish economic recovery in the third quarter of 1997 despite some improvement in major industrial sectors, a corporate survey by the Korea Chamber of Commerce said on Tuesday.

The Business Survey Index (BSI), provided by the chamber, stood at 92 for the third quarter, against 76 for the second quarter and 58 for the first. The figure less than 100 means their outlook is bearish.
"There is no doubt for the market to consolidate. If the market falls to the 740 level, institutional investors are expected to step in," Choe said.

Brokers concerned about extremely thin trading volume of 34.45 million shares as many investors clung to the sidelines. They said customers deposit at brokerage houses totalled 3.35 trillion won, while outstanding margin loans 3.3 trillion.

Banking shares fell 3.58 percent in afternoon trading after the finance ministry officially said it had decided to keep the current four percent ceiling on individual ownership in commercial banks. It closed at 384.64, down 10.41 points.
Chohung Bank shed 210 won to 5,800 with the largest trading volume of 902.19 million.

"Investors were disappointed in the news the government will not expand the ceiling," said Park Sang-jae at Coryo Securities. "They had anticipated banking shares would come into the spotlight, if the ceiling expansion signals merger and acqusition bids in the banking industry."
Seperately, the Securities Supervisory Board said 4.39 percent of Chohung Bank's outstanding common shares would become newly available for foreign investment from June 26.
Kia Motors closed unchanged at 13,400 but Kia Service shed 50 won to 6,780.

In a meeting with Finance and Economy Minister Kang Kyong-shik on Monday, Kia Group chairman Kim Sun-hong said the group is now suffering from a liquidity shortage because of continuing "malicious rumours."
A local media quoted Kang as saying the government would support Kia's efforts to normalise its management.
"It's a positive news for Kia. But investors sat on the strings," Choe said.
"It's still risky for analysts to place buy recommendation of Kia shares," said an analyst at a local securities house.

After the market close, the Securities Supervisory Board said it was considering delaying a tender offer for New Star Trading Co by Seoul-based Savoy Hotel. An watchdog official said Savoy's documentation of its takeover bid was incomplete.
-- Yeom Yoon-jeong (822) 727 5647
